content: The references provided are a collection of studies and articles that explore various strategies, interventions, and outcomes related to tuberculosis (TB) treatment adherence, management, and control. 1. Abuaku et al. (2009): This study investigated the rates of treatment default and mortality among tuberculosis patients in Hunan, China, highlighting the challenges in maintaining adherence to TB treatment protocols in this region. 2. Ershova et al. (2014): The authors evaluated adherence to national TB treatment guidelines in three provinces of South Africa, emphasizing the importance of standardized care in improving treatment outcomes. 3. Weis et al. (1994): This research examined the impact of directly observed therapy (DOT) on drug resistance and relapse rates in tuberculosis, demonstrating the effectiveness of supervised treatment in reducing these adverse outcomes. 4. Bashar et al. (2001): The study reported an increased incidence of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) among diabetic patients treated at the Bellevue Chest Service between 1987 and 1997, underscoring the need for tailored interventions in high-risk populations. 5. Ollé-Goig and Alvarez (2001): This research compared directly observed and non-observed TB treatment regimens in a rural area of Haiti, based on the experience of Hôpital Albert Schweitzer, to assess the effectiveness of supervision in improving treatment adherence. 6. Pungprassami et al. (2002): The study explored whether directly observed therapy improved TB treatment outcomes in southern Thailand, providing evidence for the benefits of supervised care in resource-limited settings. 7. Jasmer et al. (2004): This investigation compared treatment outcomes between directly observed therapy and self-administered therapy for TB patients, highlighting the advantages of supervised treatment in achieving better adherence and success rates. 8. Cavalcante et al. (2007): The authors compared community-based DOT with clinic-based models in a Brazilian favela, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of community involvement in TB care. 9. Radilla-Chávez and Laniado-Laborín (2007): This study evaluated the outcomes of DOT programs in Ensenada, Mexico, revealing that not all DOTS programs are equally effective and emphasizing the need for context-specific adaptations. 10. Anuwatnonthakate et al. (2008): The research highlighted the association between directly observed therapy and improved TB treatment outcomes in Thailand, particularly among foreign patients, by reducing treatment default rates. 11. Vieira and Ribeiro (2011): This study assessed compliance with TB treatment following the implementation of the DOTS strategy in Carapicuíba, Brazil, demonstrating significant improvements in adherence. 12. Ong’ang’o et al. (2014): The authors compared the effects of utilizing community health workers on TB treatment adherence in rural and urban settings in Kenya, showing the positive impact of community-based support. 13. Das et al. (2014): This research examined the effectiveness of directly observed versus self-administered TB treatment in a chronic conflict setting in India, providing insights into the challenges of TB care in unstable environments. 14. Alwood et al. (1994): The study evaluated the effectiveness of supervised intermittent therapy for TB in HIV-infected patients, demonstrating its potential to improve treatment outcomes in this vulnerable population. 15. Alvarez-Uría et al. (2014): This investigation compared directly observed intermittent therapy with unsupervised daily regimens during the intensive phase of TB treatment in HIV-infected patients, highlighting the benefits of supervision. 16. Juan et al. (2006): The study compared DOT for TB in pharmacies with self-administered therapy in Spain, providing evidence for the role of pharmacies in supporting TB treatment adherence. 17. Caylà et al. (2004): This research examined the current status of treatment completion and fatality rates among TB patients in Spain, identifying areas for improvement in TB care delivery. 18. Colvin et al. (2003): The authors explored the contribution of traditional healers to a rural TB control program in South Africa, emphasizing the importance of integrating traditional practices into modern TB care. 19. Singh et al. (2004): This field report from Haryana, North India, evaluated the effectiveness of urban community volunteers in directly observed TB treatment, demonstrating their potential to enhance treatment adherence. 20. Kingkaew et al. (2008): The study assessed the effectiveness of health-care workers versus family members as supervisors of TB treatment in Thailand, providing insights into the role of family involvement in TB care. 21. Tripathy et al. (2013): This research evaluated the effectiveness of community-based observation of anti-TB treatment in Bangalore City, India, highlighting the benefits of community participation in TB care. 22. Wilkinson and Davies (1997): The authors discussed the role of community supervisors in coping with Africa’s increasing TB burden, emphasizing their importance in the DOT strategy. 23. Lwilla et al. (2003): This study compared community-based versus institutional-based DOT for TB control in Tanzania, demonstrating the efficacy of community-based approaches. 24. Wandwalo et al. (2004): The authors conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of community-based DOT in an urban setting in Tanzania, providing evidence for its success. 25. Wright et al. (2004): This randomized controlled trial compared community health workers with family members as supervisors of TB treatment, highlighting the effectiveness of community health workers in improving adherence. 26. Newell et al. (2006): The study evaluated family-member DOTS and community DOTS for TB control in Nepal, demonstrating the effectiveness of both approaches in improving treatment outcomes. 27. Farmer et al. (1991): This research explored the relationship between TB, poverty, and treatment compliance in rural Haiti, providing lessons for addressing social determinants of health in TB care. 28. Jasmer et al. (2004): The authors investigated recurrent TB in the United States and Canada, distinguishing between relapse and reinfection, and providing insights into the epidemiology of TB recurrence. 29. Soares et al. (2013): This study examined TB control in a socially vulnerable area in Brazil, highlighting the need for community interventions beyond DOT to improve treatment outcomes. 30. Yassin et al. (2013): The authors reported on innovative community-based approaches in southern Ethiopia that doubled TB case notification and improved treatment outcomes, demonstrating the potential of community engagement. 31. Chan et al. (2013): This retrospective cohort study evaluated the effectiveness of a government-organized and hospital-initiated treatment program for MDR-TB patients in Taiwan, providing evidence for the success of structured care models. 32. Gärden et al. (2013): The study demonstrated that food incentives improved adherence to TB drug treatment among homeless patients in Russia, highlighting the role of social support in TB care. 33. Davidson (1998): This controlled comparison evaluated DOT versus self-administered therapy for active TB in an urban U.S. setting, providing evidence for the benefits of supervised treatment. 34. Puchalski Ritchie et al. (2015): The authors implemented a knowledge translation intervention to improve TB care and outcomes in Malawi, demonstrating the value of education and training in TB management. 35. Datiko and Lindtjorn (2009): This community-randomized trial in southern Ethiopia showed that health extension workers improved TB case detection and treatment success, emphasizing the importance of community health workers. 36. Clark et al. (2007): The study evaluated the effect of pharmacist-led patient education on adherence to TB treatment, demonstrating the positive impact of education on treatment compliance. 37. Janmeja et al. (2005): This research showed that psychotherapy improved compliance with TB treatment, highlighting the role of mental health support in TB care. 38. Liefooghe et al. (1999): The authors conducted a randomized trial to assess the impact of counseling on TB treatment adherence in Pakistan, demonstrating the benefits of psychological support. 39. Baral et al. (2014): This study emphasized the importance of providing counseling and financial support to patients receiving treatment for MDR-TB, based on mixed-method qualitative and pilot intervention studies. 40. Martins et al. (2009): The authors conducted a randomized controlled trial in Timor-Leste, showing that food incentives improved completion of TB treatment, highlighting the role of nutritional support. 41. Lutge et al. (2013): This pragmatic cluster-randomized controlled trial in South Africa evaluated the impact of economic support on TB treatment outcomes, demonstrating its effectiveness in resource-poor settings. 42. Jahnavi and Sudha (2010): This randomized controlled trial assessed the impact of food supplements on patients with newly diagnosed TB and wasting, providing evidence for the role of nutrition in TB care. 43. Sinclair et al. (2011): The Cochrane review evaluated the efficacy of nutritional supplements for people being treated for active TB, providing a comprehensive analysis of their benefits. 44. Demissie et al. (2003): This study described the use of TB clubs in rural North Ethiopia to provide community-based TB care, demonstrating the success of community participation. 45. Dick and Lombard (1997): The authors designed a health education project to enhance adherence to anti-TB treatment, emphasizing the importance of shared vision and collaboration. 46. Banerjee et al. (2000): This evaluation of a unified treatment regimen for TB in Malawi demonstrated the effectiveness of guardian-based supervision in improving treatment outcomes. 47. Becx-Bleumink et al. (2001): The study highlighted the success of community participation in achieving high TB notification and treatment success rates in Indonesia. 48. Dobler et al. (2015): This research demonstrated the success of community-based DOT in Mongolia, providing evidence for its effectiveness in improving TB treatment outcomes. 49. Dudley et al. (2003): The authors evaluated the contribution of community involvement to TB control in Cape Town, South Africa, emphasizing the importance of community engagement. 50. Maciel et al. (2010): This study compared the effectiveness of household members and health care workers as supervisors of TB treatment, providing insights into the role of family involvement. 51. Miti et al. (2003): The authors integrated TB treatment into a community-based home care program for persons living with HIV/AIDS in Zambia, demonstrating the feasibility of combined care models. 52. Moalosi et al. (2003): This cost-effectiveness analysis compared home-based care with hospital care for chronically ill TB patients in Botswana, highlighting the economic benefits of home-based care. 53. Niazi and Al-Delaimi (2003): The study assessed the impact of community participation on treatment outcomes and compliance of DOTS patients in Iraq, demonstrating the value of community involvement. 54. Wares et al. (2001): This research evaluated DOT for patients with limited access to health care facilities in Nepal, providing evidence for the success of community-mediated care. 55. Arora (2003): The study described the implementation of domiciliary DOTS in New Delhi, demonstrating the feasibility of community-mediated TB care. 56. Kironde and Meintjies (2002): The authors explored whether patient choice of supervision mattered in TB treatment delivery in high-burden settings, providing insights into patient-centered care. 57. van den Boogaard et al. (2009): This study compared community-based and facility-based DOT for TB in Tanzania, demonstrating the effectiveness of community-based approaches. 58. Manders et al. (2001): The authors investigated whether guardians could supervise TB treatment as effectively as health workers, providing evidence for the role of family members in TB care. 59. Akhtar et al. (2011): This cohort analysis evaluated DOT outcomes for TB patients in urban Pakistan, highlighting the effectiveness of supervised treatment. 60. Chuck et al. (2016): The study explored the use of video DOT to enhance TB treatment management in New York City, demonstrating the potential of technology in improving adherence. 61. Wade et al. (2012): This mixed-methods evaluation showed that home videophones improved direct observation in TB treatment, providing evidence for the use of telehealth in TB care. 62. Khortwong and Kaewkungwal (2013): The authors described a Thai health education program aimed at improving TB migrants' compliance, demonstrating the importance of targeted education. 63. Morisky et al. (1990): This patient education program aimed to improve adherence rates with anti-TB drug regimens, highlighting the role of education in TB care. 64. Drabo et al. (2009): The study described community involvement in TB care in rural Burkina Faso, demonstrating the success of community-based approaches. 65. Thiam et al. (2007): This cluster-randomized controlled trial evaluated a strategy to improve adherence to TB treatment in a resource-poor setting, providing evidence for its effectiveness. 66. Hsieh et al. (2008): The authors explored the efficacy of a case management model using DOTS in improving adherence among pulmonary TB patients, demonstrating the benefits of structured care. 67. Atkins et al. (2011): This interrupted time-series study evaluated lay health worker-supported TB treatment adherence in South Africa, providing evidence for the role of community health workers. 68. Iribarren et al. (2013): The study evaluated the acceptance and feasibility of a mobile phone-based intervention to support TB treatment adherence, demonstrating the potential of digital health tools.
